newsitem.title: USA: U.S. studying intervention in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.S. studying intervention in Zaire.

text.p: The United States is studying what role U.S. forces might play as part of a security component for a humanitarian intervention in Zaire, an administration official said on Saturday.
"There is an emerging international consensus that humanitarian intervention will be necessary to address the crisis in eastern Zaire," the official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
"There is also an emerging consensus that to be effective a humanitarian intervention will require a security component," the official said.

"We are actively studying what type of security component would be necessary for an intervention. We are also actively studying what role the U.S. might play as part of such a security component," the official said.
The United Nations Security Council early on Saturday called on U.N. members to lay the groundwork for a multinational force to help end the crisis in eastern Zaire but postponed its deployment.

The interim resolution, adopted unanimously, asked the states involved to report back as soon as possible to enable the council to give final approval. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali was asked to report to the council by November 20.

A million refugees in east Zaire have fled recent fighting between the Zairean army and Zairean ethnic Tutsis, backed by the Rwandan army. Boutros-Ghali, who has repeatedly called for swift action by the council, said the refugees were without food, water or shelter and faced starvation.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters on Friday that the United States was reviewing a variety of proposals to deal with the crisis with other nations in Africa and Europe.

But, Burns stressed: "The United States has not yet made a decision on whether or not it can and will participate in such a force, and if so, how we'll participate... -- whether it will be logistical aid or financial aid, whatever."
Diplomats have said between 4,000 and 5,000 troops would be needed to carry out the operation.

France and Spain have already said they could send 1,000 men each. However Rwanda's Tutsi government is mistrustful of France as an ally of the Hutu government ousted after genocidal massacres in 1994.
